utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. For the record, all the accused are here except for General Miletic, and for the record, also, he has communicated his waiver to the Trial Chamber. The Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon. I also notice the absence of Mr. Josse and Mr. Haynes. Do I take it that they will be showing up later in the day? I take it that they are working on other matters in the office. Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon will be joining us on Monday, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Josse will come after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And Mr. Sarapa. UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: He will be joining us in the course of the day. At the moment he's doing some other things at the office, but he will be joining us later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. From the Prosecution side, I see Mr. McCloskey and no one else. So before we bring in the witness to start his evidence, yes, I think we better go into private session for a couple of minutes. There's something I need to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, you can admit the witness. In the meantime, can you draw down the curtains until he comes in, he walks in and takes his place. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Pardon my slight appearance, but I apparently have a skin ailment of some sort. It's not the result of violence, so hopefully -- the doctor tells me it may come and go, but it's irritating but shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we noticed that two days ago, as soon as you walked in the courtroom, and we were concerned for you, Mr. McCloskey. But any time you need a break or you need some medical attention, please let us know and we'll look into that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, while we are waiting for the witness to come in and take his seat, we have put in place voice distortion for this witness, and therefore it is important that while he is addressing the Chamber, all microphones, all other microphones except his, be kept switched off. That's very important. So I will be keeping watch, keeping an open eye, but I can't see everyone at the same time, so please try to adhere to that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues, Judge Kwon, Judge Prost and Judge Stole, I wish to welcome you as a witness for the Prosecution in this case. You're familiar with the proceedings because you've already given testimony before. Madam Usher is going to hand you now the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make before you start testifying. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us that you will be testifying the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable, take a seat. What's going to happen, very simply put, is the following: Mr. McCloskey, who is lead counsel for the Prosecution in this case, will be examining you in chief, asking you a series of questions which you are about to answer truthfully. There is one -- he will then be followed by the various members of the Defence teams on cross-examination. I do not expect your testimony to finish today, but all arrangements have been put in place to accommodate you over the weekend. Now, before we continue, there's one thing I need to explain to you. You have been indicted, you have pleaded guilty or entered a guilty plea, you've been convicted and sentenced, so the usual caution that we would give to witnesses who might tend to incriminate themselves if they answer some of the questions put to you does not hold good in your case as far as the events that we're talking about, the events in Srebrenica in 1995 are concerned. So your obligation is to answer each and every question as it arises. If you do have problems, please address the Trial Chamber and we will try to deal with your remarks or complaints. Have I made myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, he is in your hands. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I direct you to line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 4. I don't believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Don't even say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be corrected later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you aware of what we're talking about, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very fine Polish investigator whose name is on the screen. I don't know how he got up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No, no. I just wanted to know whether it's the case of redacting it or just correcting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we should just correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. So it will be corrected later on. Thank you, Mr. Meek, for pointing that out to us. Mr. McCloskey, you may start and proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If, because of the voice distortion, if I could be allowed to sit down so I get that mike right, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you first just tell us your name, and spell your last for the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Drazen Erdemovic, E-r-d-e-m-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born and raised?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Tuzla. I grew up in Donja Dragunja, which is a place next to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. I notice Mr. Lazarevic. What's the problem, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have just been informed by my client that they are not receiving witness's voice in their real voice, and I'm not receiving it either. I tried already to switch off to another channel, but it doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need the technicians to attend to this before we can proceed. Now, let's -- does this apply to all the accused? Are you all in the same position or are some of you receiving the -- you are receiving it? Mr. Popovic? Mr. Nikolic? No. Mr. Borovcanin? No. Mr. Gvero, are you receiving? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I think we need the witness to say something else and check whether now the situation has been remedied. Mr. Erdemovic, can I ask you to spell out your name again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] E-r-d-e-m-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see at least two of the accused who are not receiving it. Mr. Lazarevic -- Madame Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, I have received it, but some of my colleagues have not received it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence team does not receive it either from -- none of the Defence teams are receiving it, from what I could understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that is as far as the B/C/S. I suppose you are on the right channel, all of you. I mean, I can't imagine you not to be after all these months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's hope this technical hitch is solved at the earliest. At least can you receive -- at least can you receive interpretation of what I am saying in your own language? Colonel Beara is -- yes. Can I ask the accused to speak again, say something -- the witness to say something? Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in Tuzla, and I lived in Donja Dragunja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you, Mr. Lazarevic, whether you received --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the problem? A/V TECHNICIAN: Sorry. Can I ask B/C/S booth to speak, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear the B/C/S booth, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, no one is speaking anything on B/C/S, so we cannot be sure whether we receive it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay now, Mr. Borovcanin? THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hear the witness now, but we do not hear now the interpretation from the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what I suggest is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try and have a three-minute break. In the meantime, the witness can remain in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The break is intended for everyone except the interpreters for the time being, because we need you to remain in your place so that we can try and fix this problem. Mr. Borovcanin, are you receiving now an interpretation of what I now have been saying? THE ACCUSED BOROVCANIN: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. What we are going to have, let's have a break. We are all going to stay here while this problem is being fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure also that they are receiving an interpretation of what I am saying now. Okay? Thank you. May I ask the B/C/S-speaking counsel to follow Mr. Krgovic? I just want to make sure that the B/C/S-speaking components of the Defence teams can follow now the interpretation and also the direct. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I have translation, but I have no B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is not receiving anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can follow both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you, too, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So far I'm just receiving B/C/S translation. I just have to check whether -- yes, whether -- UNIDENTIFIED SPEAKER: Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Nothing, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I hear no more complaints. Let's revert to open session now. It seems to be working fine now? Okay. Can I express the Trial Chamber's gratitude for your prompt assistance and very efficient one, for that matter, too. Thank you. So we can now proceed. Mr. McCloskey. If the problem reoccurs, please draw our attention straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's try again. Can you tell us what your ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Bosnian Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I am going to briefly outline some of the history of your legal -- your legal history here, as briefly mentioned by the Judge. On 14 January 1998, did you enter a guilty plea to one count of violation of article 3, a violation of the laws and customs of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this pursuant to a plea agreement with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were the facts underlying the charge you pled guilty to involving, well, your involvement and participation in the summary execution of Muslim men from Srebrenica on 16 July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on March 5th, 1998, were you sentenced by a Trial Chamber of this Tribunal to five years in prison?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at this time, you have served your sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have testified in the rule 61 hearing, in the Krstic trial, in the Milosevic trial; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know that your testimony in the Krstic trial was placed into evidence in the trial of Blagojevic and Jokic?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us what you were trained to do as you went through your secondary schooling?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I went to a mechanical school, mechanical engineering school in Tuzla and graduated as a locksmith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th November 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do compulsory service in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That was from December, 1990 until end March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what position did you have in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, after leaving the JNA, you have testified and stated many times that you were then in the ABiH and then the HVO and finally in the VRS. Can you give us just a brief outline --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe there are some accused who are unable to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Gvero? Thank you, Madame Fauveau. THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it broke down now, so I cannot hear the interpretation of what the Prosecutor is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, General Gvero, for pointing that out in a prompt manner. Can I ask you to repeat your question again? Say something to see whether this was transient or whether it's still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you hear me all right? Are you getting my words in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General Gvero, you're still not receiving interpretation? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] No. I can hear it, but the sound is very low, so I don't really get the meaning. It is so barely audible that I cannot really make anything out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can someone help General Gvero maybe increase the sound level? Can you receive interpretation now? Is it better? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] I can hear you, but I don't know whether I'll hear the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's got a stronger voice than mine, but let's see. Mr. McCloskey, I think you're called to the cause again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Testing 1, 2, 3. Can you hear me now? THE ACCUSED GVERO: [Interpretation] It's good now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, General Gvero, and I thank you for your patience, Mr. McCloskey. You may proceed. Make sure that all microphones are switched off, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Erdemovic, again, could you give us just a brief outline of what you did after the JNA to be involved in the ABiH, the HVO and the VRS, just briefly so we can set the scene for the 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from military service in the JNA to my hometown, the conflicts had already started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mobilisation calls started first into the Territorial Defence and later the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established. I then received a call-up to join the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I responded. I wasn't there for a long time. I was a scout with a mortar detail on Mount Mijovica. In October of the same year, 1992, I joined the military police of the HVO. I didn't stay there long, either, until November, 1993, when I transferred to Republika Srpska. In Republika Srpska, I did not join the VRS immediately. I moved to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia because of the problems that soldiers in Republika Srpska were creating for me. I joined the VRS in 1994. I believe it was in the month of April. It was a unit newly established, comprising eight to ten men under the command of the Main Staff or, rather, the Security Service of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the name of that unit at that time that you joined in '94?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was simply called "Special Unit." It didn't have a particular name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did it later become something else or get another name and develop further?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did. I believe in October, 1994, it was named 10th Sabotage Detachment, and it grew to a number of 50 or 60 men. It had two platoons, one in Vlasenica and one in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I know I asked you to give a brief outline, and I appreciate that, but let me go back just for a little more detail. Can you tell us how it was -- why did you leave the ABiH and then why did you join up with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Because I was tired of being in the battlefield, and a chance opened up for me to be with the military police and spend more time at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At that time, the HVO and the ABiH were on the same side?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us the circumstances surrounding your leaving the HVO? Why did you end up leaving the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: In the place where I used to live in Tuzla, the population was mixed. There were Muslims, Croats and Serbs. My Serb neighbours did not feel free to live there, and they asked me to help them cross a line on Mount Mijovica that I knew very well because it was the line where the HV -- it was the defence line facing Republika Srpska. In fact, they asked me to help them cross over to Republika Srpska, and that's what I did. But in doing that, I was arrested, but I cannot tell you exactly how many Serbs. I was arrested, in fact, with that group of Serbs whom I was supposed to help cross over, and the HVO arrested me. I was interrogated, mistreated. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And given that history, how was it that the VRS accepted you? Can you give us the -- I know that can be a long tale, but can you give us the abbreviated version of how that occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I was in detention, detained by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then they moved me to a detention unit held by the HVO. I talked to the commander of the military police whom I knew well, and I asked him to release me to go home to have a shower, have a change of clothes. He let me go, and I decided to cross over again to the side of Republika Srpska, to the Army of Republika Srpska, but I didn't know what would happen to me. Nobody was saying anything, nobody was explaining anything. I didn't know why I was kept in detention, because in my own understanding, I hadn't done anything bad. I just tried to help some people cross over to the side of Republika Srpska. And then I decided to cross over to Republika Srpska myself, because I knew that I hadn't done any wrong to Serbs, and I believe -- I believed that they would tell the truth. That's how I decided to move to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how was it that you signed up for the VRS, then?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the outset from November, 1993 until April, 1994, I had problems with certain units in Republika Srpska that were made up mostly of refugees from the area of Tuzla, and that's why I went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslav. However, there, in January and February, 1994, they started to mobilise Bosnian citizens who were fit for the battlefield, so I had no choice but to return to Republika Srpska. Before I arrived, I heard in Bijeljina that a unit was established, made up of Croats, Muslims and one Slovene, so I went to the military department in Bijeljina and they agreed that the best thing for me to do would be to join that unit because there are other people of my ethnicity in that unit, and that's how I decided to join that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's the unit that became the 10th Sabotage Unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to 1995. You've told us that there was two platoons of that unit, one in Vlasenica and one in Bijeljina. Which one were you in?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The one in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly how many men did that unit have at that -- in 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the whole unit or just the Bijeljina platoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just the Bijeljina platoon.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Around 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know roughly how many the Vlasenica platoon had at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I believe around the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, in 1995 what was the command structure of the unit? And start with the most highest-ranking people you know. You've said it was part of the Main Staff. Who, if anyone, did you know that had supervisory responsibility over the 10th Sabotage in 95?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from what I know and from what I was able to gather, Colonel Petar Salapura was the main man for our unit, was in charge of our unit. I knew that even back in 1994 when we were just eight or ten men. He came for meetings with us, and I saw him around, so it was Colonel Salapura. And then later I met Major Pecanac, and I just know his nickname. I have to say this in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his nickname, then?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what other command figures did you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of our unit was Second Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware of what part of the Main Staff Salapura was from?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He belonged to the Security Service. I know that he belonged to the Security Service of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you make any distinction between the Intelligence Service and the Security Service?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in our former country it all fit into the Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So let me ask you now, can you tell us, specifically in 1995, what was the function of this unit of -- in your platoon and the other platoon? What were you trained to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We were trained for sabotage jobs, going behind enemy lines, destroying hangars holding ammunition, setting explosives to blow up large-calibre weapons, destroying bridges. Sabotage activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Leading up to 1995 and in 1995, were you involved in various operations like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you about one in particular that you've talked about before. I believe -- did you go into -- make some kind of a foray into Srebrenica through a tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you did that, how many people, and what the purpose of that was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer. The question may present some lack of clarity. How many people, what do you mean? How many people were they in his contingent that took part in this foray, or do you mean to ask him something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll clarify that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, let me break it down a little bit. How many people were set aside to go on this mission from your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely how many people there were, but most of the men from my unit were there, as well as the men from the Bijeljina platoon and from the Vlasenica platoon. It was in March, 1995, if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So roughly how many men from the 10th Sabotage Detachment were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Around 30. I cannot remember precisely, but I think it was around 30 men, maybe a bit more. I can't remember better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you have any assistance from men from any other VRS units?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had men from the Bratunac Brigade or Unit, I can't remember exactly, but I believe they were from the Bratunac Brigade because they knew the mine well, and then Pelemis said they would guide us through that mine, that they know the mine, because there are many different passages and we needed guidance in order not to get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was this operation, what was the purpose of the operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose of that operation, from what I was told, was that we get in and try to start a mutiny in the ranks of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "get in," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Get in where, when you say "get in"?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: To get into the town of Srebrenica through the mine and, what do I know, fire a couple of grenades from hand-held launchers, to fire at certain targets where it was believed that there were troops of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to try to create mutiny and insurgency so that they should surrender and stop fighting for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And tell us about how the project turned out, how this operation went off, just briefly what you guys did.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We got to an elevation above the town, overlooking the town. We fired a couple of projectiles, I don't know exactly how many, from hand-held launchers, and then we were shown where the command of Nasir Oric was supposed to be, so we fired at that target. It didn't last long, maybe 10 or 15 minutes, before we pulled out and went back to Bratunac again through the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did it go off as planned or did you leave for some unforeseen reason?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any reason why we would have had to pull out. There was no firing back from the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What Mr. McCloskey meant to ask you is: Do you consider it to have been a mission completed successfully or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Did I consider it? Of course I did, but I don't know what the command decided about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As far as you knew, had you done what you were supposed to -- had the unit done what it was supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so let me take the opportunity here to ask you a couple of issues related to the practice or policy of your unit. Now, when you go into enemy lines, you obviously go through the territory of the Republika Srpska through the zone of responsibility of some VRS unit. When you did that, what, if you know, was the practice of informing or not informing the military authority of that unit that you would have been passing through?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that we had to inform the units that were holding those lines that we were going to be going on some actions in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know if your commanders had to tell the commanders of that unit what exactly you'd be doing in the enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. From what I know, they just had to inform the command of the unit that was holding the line of responsibility, but no one was told about the kind of assignment that was to be carried out. Only our command knew what kind of action was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to July of 1995, and at some point did you receive word that you were being charged with going to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of July, since our company was in the Bijeljina barracks, it was our duty every morning at 8.00 a.m. to appear -- well, if you want me to put it that way. It was like reporting to work. When I came to the barracks, I was told that we were going out on an assignment, that I should go home, that I needed to bring another uniform and everything else that I needed, personal hygiene kit and so on. I wasn't told then that we were going towards Srebrenica, but later that day I found out that we were going to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did the 10th Sabotage have at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We had a black uniform, a uniform of the Army of Republika Srpska, a uniform of the US Army, and we had a uniform that was worn by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you told or ordered what uniform to take on this operation on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think I was wearing the black uniform, and then I went home and I put the uniform that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you find out what this operation would be about?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When we arrived at Bratunac with our own vehicle, we -- when we got to Bratunac, we stopped in front of some prefabricated huts or shacks, and we learned that some people from Vlasenica were going to arrive and that together we would be going to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. McCloskey, could you please ask the witness these questions? First, in relation to the black uniform, whether that also carried any insignia. And same question in relation to the uniform -- other uniform that he put on, that is the one of the Army of Republika Srpska, did it carry the insignia of that army as well, did it show any insignia of that army as well? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First, can you describe the black uniform and whether it had any insignia on it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The black uniform was just overalls, and we had insignia that could be transferred from one uniform to another. It was the insignia of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about the camouflage uniform, the regular VRS uniform, did it have any insignia or can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a regular two-piece VRS uniform, and as I said, we had one insignia each that we were issued with, and we could move that or transfer that from one uniform to another. Mostly, when we went out on sabotage actions, we would wear no insignia. We would leave everything, insignia, our military booklet and all the other documents that we had, behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember if you wore any insignia on the Srebrenica operation of July 10th?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I did have the insignia of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and I think that on my right soldier I had a red ribbon or band, and I think we were given that when we got to the hill above Srebrenica on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to see still photographs of video of the Srebrenica operation where your colleagues were in both those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll be having some exhibits a little later, so you can describe that in more detail. Can you tell us how many -- you may have said this, but as you arrived in Bratunac, how many men were in your unit and what was the command structure? Who was there in command?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When we came to Bratunac, the people from Vlasenica still hadn't come. Franc Kos was in charge of our detachment. He waited for the others to arrive from Vlasenica and probably for Pelemis to come or Major Pecanac to issue further orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did they finally arrive?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when the Vlasenica group arrived, how many -- roughly how many total, were now from your group, the Bijeljina and the Vlasenica group, how many total 10th Sabotage people were there assembled there in Bratunac, I take it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were between 30 and 50 persons. I can't remember exactly, because some people from my unit were on another assignment. Between 30 and 40 persons, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was in command?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When the rest arrived from Vlasenica, Lule, that's his nickname, I only knew his nickname, he had more information about what would happen later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what about Pelemis; did he show up?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but Pelemis came later when we were already on the road to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what information did you learn from the person you know as Lule?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Since most of us got there by buses, they told us that trucks would be arriving to take us to Srebrenica, and not long after that this happened. I can't remember exactly, I can't explain exactly, but we didn't take the asphalt road. We went through woods, over hills. They were using hilly-terrain vehicles from the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you briefly back to this prefab building that you talked about that was in Bratunac. Do you know what kind of facility that was, military or civilian?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: From what I could see, it was a civilian facility, but it was used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And about roughly what time of day did you start off from Bratunac and go through the woods towards Srebrenica? This would be on the -- still on the 10th of July, I take it.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was late afternoon. I can't remember the exact time. It was late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go that late afternoon through those woods towards Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we went towards Srebrenica. I didn't know the terrain enough, but later I found out that, well, we came from the southern side of Srebrenica. We passed through the UN check-point. There was no one there. Then we continued towards Srebrenica, and we only stopped when we came to an elevation above Srebrenica town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened that evening of the 10th, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Pelemis appeared, and he told us that we were going to spend the night at the elevation above Srebrenica and that most probably our unit would be the first to enter the town of Srebrenica the next day, not that night. We were not going to do anything that night. We were to rest, and then in the morning we would set off to capture the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he give you an idea of what kind of resistance was expected?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can say I think that he didn't tell us at that time what exactly was expected, but he told us that the next morning, when we were preparing to go into the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly how many kilometres or less you were from the town of Srebrenica when you started off, just roughly so we can get a picture?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean, when I left from Bratunac or when we set off in the morning on the 11th towards the town?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you set off on the 11th towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that was already the outskirts of Srebrenica. I think that we were not really -- we're not talking kilometres here. These were the outskirts of Srebrenica, one of the suburbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any fire from the enemy on the night of the 10th or the early morning hours of the 11th before you actually set off?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no firing; maybe here and there, but there was no fierce fighting or shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I had interrupted you when you told us that Pelemis had, that morning of the 11th, told you something about what sort of resistance to expect. Can you tell us what he told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: He told us that we could expect strong resistance and that most probably, according to their information, the first resistance encountered could be around the first mosque as you went down into the town, which was in the southern part of the town. And he told us that we should call the civilian population to come out of their houses because we had to search the houses, and we were to send them to the stadium which was in front of us, in the direction that we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he give you any other special instructions about how to treat civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that we were not to shoot at the civilians in any case and that we were to direct them in front of us towards the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at that time did he or did you get -- well, did he give you any -- did Pelemis give you any information about any other units that would be joined with you on the attack or that were adjacent to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, he also told us that our unit, because we were the first to enter the town, would be joined by 15 persons from the Drina Wolves, and he told us -- he explained to us that the other units, once we started to descend into the town, would be giving us support, and then once we get into the town, they will start to come down from the elevations around Srebrenica. I cannot recall exactly. He said that the units from Bratunac, Milici -- I can't remember which other units he mentioned. I think I remember well the ones from Bratunac and Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your knowledge of what the Drina Wolves were?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: According to what I heard, I'm not sure, because I didn't have access to the unit, and until then I had never been in contact with that unit. I think that it was perhaps also a special unit of the Drina Corps, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a man that you knew was associated with that unit, or a nickname of a man?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Legenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was Legenda?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what I heard, I don't know exactly, but I heard that he was the commander of the unit, of the Drina Wolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe briefly what happened that morning as you set off towards Srebrenica? We're now on the morning of 11 July.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, we divided into groups. Pelemis also went with us that morning into the town. Perhaps it was already noon. I don't know exactly. For me, it was still morning. And he told us that we would be joined by the people from the Drina Wolves. As I already said, that we shouldn't shoot for no reason, that we should be calling to the people to come out of their houses. He told us not to fire at civilians. Again, it was explained that most probably there would be major resistance and that we would be the first unit to descend into the town. I don't know exactly when we set off for the town. We set off from the elevation at the southern side of Srebrenica, and to my surprise, there was -- there were no major obstacles as we were passing through the town. We came up against -- or we encountered civilians who were elderly. They had problems walking and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you ever been involved in an assault like this on a -- you know, a joint effort, as opposed to the sabotage missions you've described?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, but the people from Vlasenica who joined us had such assignments before joining our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what happens next as you encounter these older civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, Pelemis said that the first stronger resistance could appear near the first mosque. However, we reached that mosque, some elderly people, a few of them, came out of the houses, and we just told them that they should be walking in front of us and that nothing would happen to them, they should just walk in front of us. One of the soldiers, I can't remember exactly who, but I think it was Velimir Popovic, there was a flag on the mosque. He went and he took the flag down from the mosque. And we continued towards the town. Here and there, there was sporadic firing, but nothing dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you come across any military-aged men at some point, Muslim?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When we reached that -- what I thought to be the center of town, there were already buildings in the town. There was a mosque there as well. A person appeared, and from what I could see it seemed to be an able-bodied person who could be in the army. He came out, surrendered, and said that he was not in the army, that he had no problems with Serbs, had nothing against Serbs, something like that. I can't remember exactly the words. And then the people who had already started to come down from the surrounding hills -- we were already in the center of town. There was no fierce fighting, so they started to mistreat him. And not long after that, Pelemis ordered one of the soldiers from Vlasenica to go and kill that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say the people that came down from the hills started to mistreat him, which -- specifically, which people do you mean so we get a better idea?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Soldiers of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you actually hear Pelemis order that this Muslim man be killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Pelemis give this order to anyone in particular?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a soldier from the Vlasenica platoon. His name is Zoran. I know his nickname, Maljic, but I don't know his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened when Pelemis gave Zoran this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: What happened was that Zoran went off immediately and slit the throat of that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did this occur?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: In the square, from what I could tell, in the center of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What, if anything, was done with the man's body?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing was done at that point in time. Later, I returned to the southern side because Pelemis and -- told me and a few other people from my unit to return to that position where we entered town and to wait there until -- well, to secure the entrance to the town and to let him know when General Mladic passes through, which is what we did. I don't know what happened later with the body of that man. I didn't -- I wasn't in that place anymore to be able to see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us about roughly what time that murder occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It was perhaps between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m. on that day. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly about what time you took up this position that Pelemis told you about, to wait to inform him of when Mladic came through?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: It could have been about 2.00 or 3.00. I don't know. I cannot remember the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Mladic come through that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly, again just roughly, I know this -- what time Mladic came through?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact time, but I know that it wasn't much later after we returned to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did he travel through? Was he in vehicles or on foot?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Vehicles passed. I think there were three vehicles. Mladic was in the first one. I think there was a Praga, that's what we called it in the army, that was going or moving ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, this might be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Haynes has -- is now present in the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, before we continue the -- with the events from 11 July, I want to go back to a topic, and I know it's been a long time since you've thought and talked about a lot of this material, so I want to read you a couple of answers that you have given on a topic and see if that helps refresh your recollection. It's about the position of Mr. Salapura. So let's just take a second here, and I'm sure you recall speaking to Jean Rene Ruez, well, a few times, but I'm speaking of the April, 1996 interview, and he asked you at one point: "Do you know who was above Lieutenant Pelemis?" This is page 8 of the English. And your answer was: "Colonel Salapura." And Mr. Ruez said: "Colonel Salapura was constantly present inside the unit or did he only appear in some specific circumstances?" Your answer was: "He was in the Intelligence Centre of the main chief command and we saw him very rarely and only on specific occasions." Now, let me go to the Krstic trial of 22 May where Mr. Harmon asked you the following on page 3079: "I'd like you to then identify some of the hierarchy of the 10th Sabotage Detachment as you knew it in July of 1995. Could you please tell us, from the highest levels working down to the level of Franc Kos and Lule, what was the reporting chain of command?" And your answer was: "As far as I know, in the first place there was Colonel Salapura from the Main Staff, the Intelligence Centre. He was there from the beginning, when there were eight of us, and later on as well." Having heard that, does that refresh your recollection a bit better about the position of Salapura?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I said here this morning earlier, I was trying to find the words in Serbo-Croatian to explain it, but unfortunately, I have little contact nowadays with people who speak Serbo-Croatian, and I have difficulty finding the words, and that's why I was trying to find the simplest way of putting things. But that's correct, he was with the Intelligence Centre, and the Security Service is the same thing for me, because when I was with the JNA, it used to be the Security Service, and we used to call all the people engaged in intelligence work security men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. But you can be clear now that you have said to Mr. Ruez, you've testified -- in fact, I think you've always said that Mr. Salapura was an intelligence officer. Is that your memory now?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. But as I said, I tried to formulate that earlier this morning. I couldn't remember the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, no problem. Now, I believe we left off where you had said that General Mladic did go through your check-point in the southern part of town in vehicles. Can you just describe to us briefly what happened the rest of that day on the 12th, if anything in particular? Excuse me, that's the 11th.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The 11th. Well, not much was happening, as far as my unit is concerned. Most of us remained closer to the south side of the town, looking from the center, where we set up that check-point, a security check-point, so that General Mladic can enter the town in safety. At one point, one of my colleagues and I set out towards the center, and then we encountered several soldiers from my unit, and there were also several persons whom I didn't know. They were drinking Sljivovica from a plastic jerry can. We started talking. One of the soldiers who belonged to my unit gave me a -- or rather gave that person at the check-point a hand-held launcher, the person whom I didn't know. I asked him, "Why did you give that to him?" And he said, "He's going to be retired soon." And I asked, "Who is it?" And they answered that it was General Zivanovic. One person from my unit said, "He's not a general, he's a drunk."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what else happened that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Then I heard that some of the units asked Pelemis about checking that mine, one entrance to which was in Srebrenica and the other entrance was on the Bratunac side. I cannot recall the name now, but one of the commanders of a brigade from the Zvornik Corps asked Pelemis, since we already knew that mine, that our unit be assigned to check those pits, and that's why we were told to stay overnight in Srebrenica the night of the 11th. Nothing much was happening that I could see. However, Pelemis and individuals from Vlasenica were not there with us. They showed up later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did Pelemis show back up?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Pelemis appeared early in the evening. He didn't stay long. He just said that we split into two groups, to stay in two different houses, and the next day we would go to check that mine. And then he left with his driver. His driver and he did not spend the night in Srebrenica. There was only with us the commander of the Vlasenica platoon and the commander of the Bijeljina platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you spend the night in those two houses?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly describe what you did the next day, very briefly, if you could.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, nothing happened. We just waited for Pelemis to come the next day so that we can go and check those pits. However, when Pelemis did come, we were told that we were not going to do that, after all, that we were going back to Vlasenica instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt you, Mr. McCloskey, but since we've moved now to the 12th, I would like to know from the witness whether at any time during the 11th, while he and his platoon are there in Srebrenica in the centre of town, whether they could see any inhabitants of Srebrenica around or was it a ghost town at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you describe any -- could you answer the Judge's question? Did you see any Muslims, any civilians, aside -- you've described briefly, but could you give us more information on what you would have seen or not seen related to civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The only civilians I saw were those who came out of their homes when we called to them. Perhaps 200 persons. Those were the only civilians I saw in Srebrenica, including that civilian who was killed. They were the only ones that I saw. I didn't see any more civilians until that thing that happened at Branjevo Farm on the 16th. Later on, when I came to The Hague, I was shown videotapes, and only then did I realise that there had been civilians in Potocari, because I didn't know that area well at all, I didn't know that place was called Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us about roughly how many civilians came out of buildings, as you've described, and that you sent up towards the soccer field on the other end of town?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I just said a moment ago that it was around 200 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that evening, when you were staying in the two buildings, did any Muslims come by or did you see any Muslims on the street, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't see any civilians at all. Nobody even talked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think I'll now ask you to -- you've seen, over the years, video and photographs. I want to go over some what were photographs from the Krstic exhibits that you had identified. And the first one, if we could have 65 ter 1966. Now, these were from the Krstic trial, and so their quality is perhaps a little different than the quality that we've seen on the video, but have you had a chance yesterday to actually see the video that these stills were taken from to help your recollection and your confirmation of these stills?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Stills? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before he answers the question, Witness, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, it doesn't really make a difference, but before we show him these stills, I understand that at least one of these stills has got some yellow markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The first one has a yellow dot, but I don't think it really gives anything away or -- and it's something he's talked about before in the other trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections on the part of the Defence teams? We hear none. Okay, then we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Okay. We now see this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the fellow with the -- well, it's obviously been -- we put on that yellow dot years ago. Do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know what unit he's from?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was from my unit, the 10th Sabotage Detachment, but he was in the Vlasenica platoon. I know his nickname, Cico. He would sometimes serve as the driver to our commander, Milomir Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 1979.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before we do so, the gear that he's wearing there, the camouflage trousers and a kind of a T-shirt or vest, was that part of the uniform of the Vlasenica platoon or is he wearing casual -- partly casual clothes?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, from what I can remember, he never went on missions, he never went into action. He was always in the rear, and he was always dressed like that. And that's how he was dressed when he served as a driver to the commander of our detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, go ahead, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Those camouflage pants that he's wearing, are those like the camouflage pants you would have worn in your camo gear that you described?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Those uniforms were mostly in the Vlasenica platoon. It comes from the Greek army, and the Vlasenica platoon had most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you see that helmet he's got in his left hand? Did you get a better look at that helmet in another picture from the video?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where that helmet came from?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: It's a helmet from the UN soldiers. It had been taken from one armoured vehicle that Cico and some other men from our unit appropriated for our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next photograph, 65 ter 1979. Now, we see a UN vehicle off the side of the road and an individual. Before I ask you about the individual, do you know if you were on this particular road or was that not a place that you guys went, if you can tell at all where this road is?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, this place does not mean anything to me. I don't recognize it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you never would have gone by this UN vehicle that's stuck on the side of the road?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember passing by. I did pass by the UN base that was located on the south side, but I didn't see a single vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you about this man again who has a yellow dot that's been put on the photograph. Do you recognise the man in this picture?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who is he?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: He was the radio operator in our unit, but he belonged to the Vlasenica platoon. I know him by nickname. I don't know his real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's his nickname?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Bujo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the uniform he's wearing, can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That uniform belonged to our unit. It was the black one. And if I may just say, on the left arm he's wearing the insignia of our unit. I believe that's the one, because it's white.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I know that's not a great picture of the insignia, but can you just describe -- just describe the insignia, if you can. What's it of?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: All I can remember is that it was written on it "10th Sabotage Detachment," and there was a white eagle. I cannot be sure now. It's been a long time since I last saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one, 1978. Now, this is not a great quality, but having seen the video and seeing this shot, can you give us any help on who these people are?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The person who is closer to the UN armoured vehicle, it's my assumption, but I saw the photograph and I know that it is Cico, and the other one is also a signalsman who served with the Vlasenica platoon, but I cannot remember his name, nor even his nickname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try to clarify this. The guy who is wearing what appears to be a blue helmet, who -- is that Cico?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next shot, 65 ter 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This man in the forefront with the rifle stock in his back, do you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a person from the Vlasenica platoon. His name is Zoran Stupar. He was logistics man in the Vlasenica platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next one, 65 ter 1980. This will be a photograph where three men are numbered in yellow, 1, 2, 3, that you have previously identified. I'll ask you, if you can by number, if you can recall, who they were.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is Bujo, the signalsman in our unit, from the Vlasenica platoon. Number 2 was also a signalsman with our unit, also from the Vlasenica platoon. Number 3, from what I can remember, is Cico, who was also in our unit. He served as a driver to our detachment commander, and "Cico" was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Number 2, had you seen him in the previous -- in one of the previous photographs?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is he the person whose name you didn't know that was standing next to the person with the blue helmet?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to 65 ter 1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you do so. We have seen a sequence of photos in which this Cico sometimes appearing either carrying or wearing a blue helmet, other times not. The witness said that he recalls this Cico having procured such helmet or helmets. Can he tell us whether the procurement of such helmets occurred before this instance or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know anything about how he procured -- how he got this helmet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, would he have had it before this occasion already?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where this is, which place this is where this is happening, but I assume that he most probably found the helmet in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can play this segment of the video - it's lined up - if you would like. It may make more sense, but it would take some time. I don't know if you want to see it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. For the time being, let's proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think I'd called up 65 ter 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we see three people in what appear to be black uniforms, numbered 1, 2, 3. Number 1, do you know who that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a person from my unit. He belonged to the Bijeljina platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Velimir Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And number 2, he is a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He belonged to the Vlasenica platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you have never given us his name; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly why?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Because that person is quite -- how can I explain it? That person did not take part in anything that was not permitted, and because above all, he was very pleasant to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I won't go any further than that. Number 3, do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Number 3, yes, that's a person from my unit. He was in the Bijeljina platoon. His name is Stanko Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, the person on the far left in the camouflage uniform, at the time did you ever see that person around Srebrenica at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No. Now I know it's General Krstic. I even testified in his case. But I emphasise that I didn't have any contacts with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, now I don't have any more of those photographs. Let's go to the 12th. And I think you talked briefly about it. Can you take up where you left off? What happened on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: As I already said, when Pelemis, the commander of our detachment, returned to Srebrenica, he said that the mine does not need to be searched, that we should pack and go back to Vlasenica, which is what we did. I cannot remember exactly when we started to go back to Vlasenica, but I know that we went via a surface mine in Milici, taking a road through the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get anywhere near Potocari on your way towards Milici and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you learn about anything happening to anyone on the 12th? Was there some sort of accident?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The vehicle that I was in, on the way from Srebrenica to Vlasenica, broke down, so that we stayed behind for a few hours. I can't remember how long, but we stayed behind for a long time until the vehicle was fixed. And then when we got to Vlasenica, we found out that the UN transporter had overturned, and it was driven by the commander of our unit, Pelemis, and that one of the soldiers perished. This was not far from the Vlasenica base, which was in the Dragasevac Place. It's on the road from Vlasenica towards Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the name of this soldier that died in the accident?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Kolibrat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had he been one of the soldiers involved in the Srebrenica operation with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you receive -- what was your next assignment that you received after getting back to the base at Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: When we came back to Vlasenica, we heard what happened to Kolibrat, Dragan, and then in the morning -- actually, in the night, we didn't know anything about that was happening, and then when we got up in the morning on the 13th, Dragan Kolibrat, who was from the Bijeljina platoon, and then in the morning the logistics guys from the Vlasenica platoon, I think it was Zoran Stupar who came and said that I and a few other people should go to the funeral in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where is Trebinje from Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Trebinje is to the south. It's close to the Republic of Croatia, near the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe that trip, who you went with, when you went, how long you stayed?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We went on the 13th. If the situation was quiet, it wouldn't take long to get there. However, that particular trip took much longer than it would take before the war when you travelled, because we had to take a detour in the mountains around Sarajevo and the roads were quite bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many of you went?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Six or seven. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long were you there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Like I said, it took us almost all day on the 13th to get there. The funeral was on the 14th. We set off late on the 14th, late at night, on our return, and the journey back also took a long time, and it was during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What day did you come back?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th, in the early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We came to Vlasenica. We went to sleep. We were tired from the trip and the funeral and everything. We didn't sleep. We were on alert, practically speaking, from the 10th until the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened, if anything, on the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the morning, we were in one of the rooms where the beds were for resting. Brano Gojkovic came and said that I, Franc Kos, Zoran Goronja should get our weapons ready and prepare to go for an assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We did that, and maybe after half an hour we set off from Dragasevac, our unit's base, towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many people?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you name those people?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: I, Brano Gojkovic, Zoran Svetkovic, who was driving the vehicle, Marko Boskic, Golijan -- I can't remember his first name -- Zoran Goronja, Franc Kos, and Stanko Savanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his rank, if any?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: From what I know, he didn't have a rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your rank or position at that time in the unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, I was a corporal in the Army of Republika Srpska. I was a corporal in the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and because of conflicts between me and Milorad Pelemis, who was the commander of our unit, he stripped me of the rank. I was actually the commander of a group in the Bijeljina platoon, but at that moment I was just a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know who had given Brano Gojkovic the command of this unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: He said that Pelemis came and said to get ready, so I conclude, on the basis of that, that Pelemis told Brano what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before you left on this assignment, did you see any officers like Pelemis or anyone above him around Vlasenica, where you guys were staying?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, Pelemis was there, but the night when we returned to Vlasenica from Srebrenica, this was on the 12th at night, Major Pecanac was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had -- could you tell whether or not Pelemis had been -- had any kind of injury?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: All I know is that he had a bandage -- plaster Band-Aid on his forehead, because he had overturned in the UN armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to your departure with this group of men that you've named. Who was driving this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Svetkovic was driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have asked you this, but could you describe the vehicle and its colour?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Volkswagen van, green in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We went in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you first stop?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: We stopped not far from the exit to Zvornik. There was some buildings there. We stopped near a gate somewhere there, and then Brano was the first one to go inside, and he talked with the military police who were in that kind of building near this gate, and they allowed our vehicle to enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If we could bring up 65 ter 1915. Do you recognise what's depicted on this photo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: These are the buildings, the compound with the buildings, where we went in on that day, the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could go to the next photo, which is a bit of a closer-up. It's 65 ter 1916. And I'm going to be asking him to make some markings on this. There's a new piece of equipment that will allow you to mark on this, this screen. Looking at this photo that is up there, is that the place you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
